The central argument against continued American submission to organizations like the United Nations and the World Trade Organization is simple: the American people, through their Constitution, are supposed to govern the United States. Laws and policies affecting Americans should be made by elected officials accountable to American voters—not by international bureaucrats, foreign judges, diplomatic committees, or multilateral panels.

The United States was founded on the principle of popular sovereignty. Government derives its legitimacy from the consent of the governed. International organizations, however, often operate outside that principle. Their officials are not elected by Americans. Their procedures are remote and bureaucratic. Their decisions are frequently shaped by coalitions of countries whose values, interests, and political systems are fundamentally different from America’s.

This creates a democratic deficit. When American policy is influenced or constrained by institutions in which authoritarian governments, anti-American blocs, and unaccountable bureaucrats have a voice, American citizens lose control over their own national destiny. Even when such organizations lack direct enforcement power, they can still pressure the United States diplomatically, economically, and legally. Over time, this erodes the expectation that America is a sovereign republic whose policies are determined at home.

The United Nations Has Failed Its Own Mission

The United Nations is often defended as a guardian of peace, but its record is deeply flawed. It has not prevented major wars. It has not stopped genocide consistently. It has not eliminated tyranny. It has not ensured that aggressor states are meaningfully restrained. Instead, the UN often provides a stage on which hostile regimes can posture, condemn the United States and its allies, and shield themselves behind diplomatic procedure.

The UN Security Council is structurally paralyzed by the veto power of permanent members, including Russia and China. This means that some of the world’s most powerful authoritarian states can block meaningful action against themselves or their allies. As a result, the UN frequently cannot act decisively when action is most needed. It becomes a forum for speeches rather than solutions.

Worse, UN bodies have repeatedly given legitimacy to regimes with atrocious human rights records. Organizations supposedly dedicated to human rights have included or elevated states that suppress dissent, persecute minorities, jail political opponents, restrict religious freedom, and censor speech. When governments that violate basic liberties are allowed to sit in judgment of free nations, the institution loses moral credibility.

The United States contributes significant funding to the UN system, yet receives little in return that could not be accomplished through direct alliances, regional partnerships, or independent diplomacy. America does not need the permission of the UN to defend itself, trade with allies, provide humanitarian aid, or oppose aggression. When the UN supports American goals, it is often redundant. When it opposes them, it becomes an impediment.

The WTO Has Not Protected American Workers

The World Trade Organization was promoted as a rules-based system that would open markets, reduce unfair trade barriers, and create prosperity. In practice, it has often failed to protect American workers and industries from predatory economic behavior by other countries. The WTO model assumes that member states will compete according to shared rules and that violations can be handled through dispute procedures. But that assumption breaks down when major economies manipulate markets, subsidize strategic industries, exploit labor, steal intellectual property, or use state-directed capitalism while still claiming the benefits of open trade.

The United States opened its markets under the expectation that others would do the same fairly. But American manufacturing communities have suffered from decades of outsourcing, industrial decline, and trade imbalances. While free trade can benefit consumers through lower prices, trade policy should not be judged by cheap goods alone. A nation must also preserve its productive capacity, technological edge, supply-chain security, and middle-class employment base.

The WTO has too often treated American efforts to defend domestic industries as suspect while failing to adequately discipline countries that engage in systematic unfair practices. It has constrained the ability of the United States to use tariffs, procurement rules, and industrial policy to defend its workers. That is unacceptable. Trade rules should serve the American economy, not the other way around.

A sovereign nation must be able to decide what industries are essential, what trade relationships are secure, and what measures are needed to protect its citizens. If WTO commitments prevent the United States from rebuilding manufacturing, protecting critical supply chains, or responding forcefully to unfair competition, then those commitments should be abandoned.

International Organizations Often Empower America’s Rivals

A major flaw in many global institutions is that they give adversarial or authoritarian states access, legitimacy, and influence without requiring genuine political reform. Countries that oppose American interests can use international organizations to constrain the United States while ignoring rules themselves. They gain the benefits of participation—diplomatic legitimacy, market access, procedural influence—without adopting American standards of transparency, liberty, or fair competition.

This dynamic is especially dangerous because the United States often takes treaty obligations, institutional norms, and legal commitments seriously. Many rivals do not. America binds itself while others maneuver around the rules. The result is not a fair international order; it is strategic self-limitation.

International organizations are frequently described as neutral, but neutrality can become a weapon when it refuses to distinguish between free societies and oppressive regimes, between defensive alliances and aggressive powers, or between market economies and state-controlled systems. If America’s rivals can use these institutions to slow, shame, sue, or isolate the United States, then continued participation becomes a strategic liability.

American Alliances Do Not Require Global Bureaucracy

Opponents of withdrawal often argue that leaving institutions like the UN or WTO would mean embracing isolationism. This is a false choice. The United States can remain deeply engaged in the world without submitting to broad multilateral bureaucracies.

America should cooperate with nations when cooperation serves mutual interests. It should maintain strong alliances, negotiate bilateral and regional trade agreements, support freedom of navigation, share intelligence with trusted partners, and provide aid when doing so advances clear objectives. None of this requires deference to the UN General Assembly or WTO panels.

In fact, smaller and more focused partnerships are often more effective than large global institutions. A coalition of committed allies can act faster and with greater unity than a universal organization that includes dictatorships, rivals, and hostile states. Trade agreements can be negotiated directly with countries that respect fair competition. Security cooperation can be handled through alliances based on shared interests and capabilities. Humanitarian work can be conducted through American agencies, private charities, religious organizations, and trusted partners.

The issue is not whether America should engage with the world. It should. The issue is whether America should allow global institutions to define the terms of that engagement. It should not.

The Financial Burden Is Unjustified

American taxpayers should not be expected to bankroll institutions that frequently oppose American priorities or provide platforms for anti-American rhetoric. Funding international organizations may be justified when they produce clear benefits. But when they become bloated, politicized, ineffective, or hostile to US interests, continued funding becomes irresponsible.

Every dollar sent to international bureaucracies is a dollar not spent securing the border, modernizing the military, rebuilding infrastructure, supporting veterans, strengthening domestic industry, or reducing the burden on taxpayers. The United States should evaluate international commitments the same way it evaluates any public expenditure: does this serve the American people? If the answer is no, the funding should end.

Defenders of the current system often speak as if American support for global institutions is a moral obligation. It is not. The first duty of the American government is to the American people. International spending must be justified by national benefit, not diplomatic habit.

Withdrawal Would Restore Accountability

One of the strongest reasons to withdraw from or dismantle these organizations is that doing so would restore responsibility to American elected officials. Politicians often use international commitments as excuses for unpopular decisions. They claim that trade rules, global norms, climate agreements, security resolutions, or diplomatic obligations require certain policies. This allows them to shift blame away from themselves and toward distant institutions.

Withdrawal would remove that excuse. If American leaders want open trade, foreign aid, military intervention, sanctions, refugee commitments, or regulatory harmonization, they should argue for those policies directly before the American people. They should not hide behind international consensus.

Self-government requires accountability. Accountability requires that citizens know who is making decisions. International organizations blur that line. A republic should not be governed through vague obligations to global bodies; it should be governed through constitutional processes that voters can understand and influence.

A Better Path: Sovereign Cooperation

The United States should pursue a new model: sovereign cooperation. This means cooperating internationally where useful, but rejecting any arrangement that compromises constitutional authority, economic independence, or national security.

Under such a model, America would:

  • Withdraw from organizations that consistently undermine US sovereignty or interests.
  • Defund international bodies that promote anti-American agendas or fail basic accountability tests.
  • Replace broad multilateral commitments with bilateral and regional agreements.
  • Rebuild domestic manufacturing and protect critical industries.
  • Work with allies through flexible coalitions rather than universal bureaucracies.
  • Reserve the right to impose tariffs, sanctions, and restrictions when American security or prosperity requires it.
  • Reject international legal claims that conflict with the Constitution or the decisions of American voters.

This is not isolationism. It is realism. It recognizes that international institutions are not sacred. They are tools. When a tool no longer works, a responsible nation replaces it.

Conclusion

The United States should no longer treat membership in organizations like the United Nations and World Trade Organization as an unquestionable good. These institutions may have been created with ambitious hopes, but their modern performance does not justify continued American deference. They dilute sovereignty, empower rivals, constrain economic policy, waste taxpayer money, and often fail to deliver the peace, fairness, or cooperation they promise.

America’s strength has never come from permission granted by international bodies. It has come from constitutional liberty, economic dynamism, military power, technological innovation, and the consent of its citizens. Those foundations must not be subordinated to global bureaucracies that Americans cannot vote out and that do not reliably serve American interests.

The United States should engage the world confidently, but on its own terms. It should trade, negotiate, aid, deter, and cooperate as a sovereign republic—not as a subordinate member of a managerial global order. Withdrawing from or actively dismantling ineffective and sovereignty-eroding institutions would not weaken America. It would restore the principle that American policy must be made by Americans, for Americans, in the service of the American nation.

Reclaiming American Sovereignty: The Case for Withdrawal from International Institutions

For nearly eighty years, the United States has operated under the assumption that global institutions like the United Nations and the World Trade Organization serve American interests. This assumption deserves rigorous scrutiny rather than reflexive acceptance. A compelling case exists that these organizations have evolved into structures that constrain American decision-making, redistribute American resources to nations hostile to US interests, and subordinate the will of American voters to unelected international bureaucracies.

The Constitutional Argument for Sovereignty

The United States Constitution establishes a clear framework: sovereignty resides in the American people, exercised through elected representatives accountable to voters. International organizations, by design, dilute this accountability. When the UN General Assembly votes—where the United States holds the same single vote as nations with fractions of its population, economic output, or commitment to democratic governance—American interests get outvoted by coalitions of authoritarian states and their client governments.

The WTO's dispute resolution mechanisms have historically allowed unelected panels to rule against American laws passed by Congress and signed by presidents. When international bodies can effectively override domestic legislation, they create a shadow governance structure unaccountable to American voters. This represents a genuine transfer of sovereign authority to entities with no democratic accountability to the American public.

The UN's Record of Anti-American Bias

Critics point to a consistent pattern: the UN Human Rights Council has included and been shaped by nations with abysmal human rights records, while disproportionately targeting Israel, America's closest Middle East ally, with condemnations exceeding those directed at far more egregious human rights violators. The UN Security Council remains structurally paralyzed by veto powers held by Russia and China, nations actively working against American strategic interests, rendering the institution incapable of decisive action precisely when action matters most.

Meanwhile, the United States shoulders a disproportionate share of UN funding—historically around 22% of the regular budget and closer to 25-28% of peacekeeping costs—while wielding influence proportionally diminished by the one-nation-one-vote structure in the General Assembly. Proponents of withdrawal argue this represents an enormous transfer of American taxpayer wealth for diminishing strategic return.

Economic Sovereignty and the WTO

The WTO's framework, defenders of withdrawal argue, has enabled a hollowing-out of American manufacturing by normalizing trade relationships with nations like China that manipulate currency, subsidize state industries, and ignore intellectual property protections while receiving most-favored-nation status. China's WTO accession in 2001 was supposed to liberalize its economy; instead, critics argue, it provided China cover to pursue mercantilist policies while American factories closed and manufacturing communities collapsed.

The WTO's binding dispute mechanisms mean American trade policy—tariffs, subsidies, regulatory standards—can be challenged and effectively overturned by international panels weighing "free trade" principles against American economic security interests, environmental standards, or labor protections that Congress and the executive branch determined were in the national interest.

The Path Forward: Bilateral Strength Over Multilateral Constraint

Advocates for withdrawal argue that America's economic and military power gives it far more leverage in direct, bilateral negotiations than in multilateral forums where that power gets diluted by design. A United States unconstrained by WTO adjudication could pursue trade policy calibrated precisely to American interests—protecting strategic industries, responding immediately to unfair trade practices, and negotiating terms nation-by-nation from a position of strength rather than submitting to one-size-fits-all multilateral frameworks.

Similarly, withdrawal from UN structures wouldn't mean American isolation—it would mean pursuing American diplomatic, humanitarian, and security objectives through coalitions of genuinely aligned democratic allies (NATO, bilateral defense treaties, ad hoc coalitions) rather than institutions structurally captured by adversarial blocs.

A Necessary Counterpoint

Reclaiming America's Destiny: Why the United States Must Actively Withdraw from and Dismantle the United Nations and World Trade Organization

The United States of America was founded on a radical idea: that a sovereign people, governed by their own Constitution and accountable only to their own citizens, could chart a course for human liberty and prosperity unmatched in history. That sovereignty is now under systematic assault from the very international organizations the U.S. helped create. The United Nations and the World Trade Organization do not merely fail to advance American interests—they actively undermine them, erode constitutional self-government, transfer power to unaccountable foreign bureaucrats, and subsidize adversaries at American expense. The time has come for the United States to withdraw from these institutions and pursue their systematic dismantlement. Anything less is a betrayal of American independence.

The Assault on Sovereignty

Sovereignty is not an abstract concept. It means the American people, through their elected representatives, retain the final say over their laws, borders, military, economy, and culture. Both the UN and WTO directly attack this principle.

The United Nations was sold to the American public as a mechanism for world peace. In practice, it has become a permanent diplomatic albatross that dilutes American power. The General Assembly routinely passes resolutions condemning the United States and its democratic ally Israel while remaining largely silent on genuine atrocities committed by authoritarian regimes. More dangerously, UN treaties and conventions attempt to impose international standards on everything from gun control to parental rights to climate policy. These efforts create pressure for judicial interpretation that treats "evolving international norms" as superior to the U.S. Constitution.

The UN's specialized agencies consistently work against American values. UNESCO has a documented history of anti-Western bias. The Human Rights Council routinely includes some of the world's worst human rights abusers as members, allowing them to lecture democracies. When the UN involves itself in "peacekeeping," it often creates dependencies and corruption rather than resolution. The organization has become a global forum in which dictatorships have equal voting weight with the world's oldest constitutional republic.

The World Trade Organization represents an even more direct transfer of sovereignty. Its dispute settlement system allows foreign governments to challenge American laws, regulations, and tariffs before panels of unelected judges whose decisions the United States is expected to obey. This is not trade policy. It is the subordination of American self-government to an international trade court. When the U.S. attempts to protect its industries or workers from predatory practices, particularly from China, it faces WTO complaints and the threat of retaliatory sanctions blessed by an organization that consistently fails to address currency manipulation, intellectual property theft, and forced technology transfer.

The WTO's rules were written for a world that no longer exists—one in which all major economies played by roughly similar rules and sought mutual benefit. That world died the moment China was allowed to join in 2001. The organization now primarily serves to constrain America's ability to respond to economic warfare while providing cover for systematic violations by others.

These Institutions Do Not Serve American Interests

The argument that these organizations serve American interests collapses under examination.

The United States is the largest financial contributor to the United Nations by a wide margin, providing roughly 22% of the regular budget and far more for peacekeeping and specialized programs. This money funds an organization that frequently opposes American foreign policy, criticizes American constitutional rights, and provides diplomatic cover for America's adversaries. American taxpayers effectively subsidize anti-American diplomacy.

The UN has failed at its core mission of maintaining international peace. It could not prevent the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the Chinese threat to Taiwan, or Iran's nuclear ambitions. Instead, it often serves as a platform for those very regimes to isolate the United States diplomatically. The organization's refugee policies and migration compacts have consistently pushed policies that encourage mass migration into Western nations while doing little to address root causes in failing states.

The WTO has presided over the greatest transfer of wealth and industrial capacity in human history—from the United States and Europe to China. America's manufacturing base was hollowed out under WTO rules that made it nearly impossible to respond to dumping, subsidies, and mercantilist practices. The organization has proven structurally incapable of addressing China's economic model, which combines state capitalism, military-civil fusion, and systematic rule-breaking. The result has been American unemployment in once-thriving industrial regions, strategic dependence on a geopolitical rival for critical supply chains, and the enrichment of the Chinese Communist Party.

The Founders Warned Us

The American Founders understood the dangers of entangling alliances and supranational authority. George Washington's Farewell Address remains prophetic: "It is our true policy to steer clear of permanent alliances with any portion of the foreign world." Thomas Jefferson warned against "entangling alliances." They designed a constitutional system in which sovereignty resided with the American people, exercised through representative government—not delegated to foreign capitals or international bureaucracies.

Modern international organizations represent the very kind of distant, unaccountable power that the American Revolution was fought to escape. The difference is that instead of a king in London, power now resides in conference rooms in Geneva and New York filled with diplomats who have no loyalty to American citizens.

The Path Forward: Withdrawal and Dismantlement

The United States should immediately announce its intention to withdraw from both organizations and work actively to dismantle their influence.

For the United Nations, this means ending all mandatory funding, withdrawing from all optional protocols and conventions that constrain American policy, and encouraging like-minded nations to build alternative frameworks based on genuine national sovereignty rather than global governance. Bilateral and regional alliances based on shared interests and values should replace multilateral theater.

For the WTO, the United States should withdraw and pursue reciprocal bilateral trade agreements that prioritize American workers, strategic independence, and fair competition. Tariffs and trade policy should be set by the American people through their elected representatives, not foreign bureaucrats. The goal should not be isolation but selective engagement that serves American interests without subordinating them.

The inevitable objections—that this represents "isolationism" or that America cannot "go it alone"—are intellectually dishonest. No serious advocate of withdrawal argues for ending all diplomacy, trade, or alliances. Strong bilateral relationships with nations that share American interests, whether on security, technology, or economics, would replace the current system. The United States remains the world's largest economy and preeminent military power. It does not need permission from international organizations to protect its citizens or advance its interests.

The claim that these organizations provide essential global public goods is equally unpersuasive. Global coordination on truly mutual concerns—such as certain infectious diseases or maritime navigation—can occur through narrower, purpose-built agreements that do not require subordinating American sovereignty to permanent bureaucracies with expansive mandates.

A Renewal of American Sovereignty

Withdrawing from and working to dismantle the UN and WTO would not diminish America—it would liberate it. It would restore the constitutional principle that American laws are made by Americans. It would redirect resources from institutions that often work against American interests toward direct bilateral relationships based on reciprocity and realism. Most importantly, it would signal to the world, and to the American people themselves, that the United States intends to remain a sovereign republic rather than a mere component in someone else's vision of global governance.

The American experiment has always been based on the revolutionary notion that self-governing peoples are superior to empires, monarchies, and transnational bureaucracies. The current international architecture represents a reversion to pre-American thinking: that experts in distant capitals know better than citizens and their representatives. The United Nations and World Trade Organization are symptoms of this regression.

It is time to end the experiment in subordinating American sovereignty to international institutions. The United States should lead the world out of these failing organizations by leaving them—and working to ensure they no longer constrain the freest, most successful nation in history. American sovereignty is not a problem to be managed. It is a principle to be reclaimed. The survival of the American republic requires nothing less.

Arguments for US Withdrawal from or Dismantling the UN and WTO

Proponents of reduced US involvement—particularly advocates of “America First” or national-sovereignty-centered foreign policy—argue that these organizations constrain the United States in three core areas: sovereignty, economic interests, and bureaucratic efficiency. Below is a structured summary of the main claims.

1. Sovereignty and National Independence

The central argument is that the United States sacrifices decision-making autonomy when it submits to international institutions in which it holds minority influence.

  • United Nations: The US is the largest financial contributor (roughly 22% of the regular budget and historically around 25% of peacekeeping) but holds only one vote in the 193-member General Assembly. Critics argue this creates an inversion of power: American resources subsidize an institution that frequently passes resolutions condemning US allies (especially Israel) or pushing norms on migration, arms control, or human rights that conflict with US domestic policy or constitutional prerogatives. The UN Charter’s collective-security framework is said to entangle the US in conflicts or constrain its freedom of action (e.g., debates over “legality” of military operations that bypass the Security Council). Withdrawal would, in this view, restore the principle that only the US Constitution and elected officials—not international bureaucrats or hostile voting blocs—determine American foreign policy.

  • World Trade Organization: WTO dispute-settlement panels and its former Appellate Body are accused of acting as a supra-national court that can declare US trade remedies (tariffs, countervailing duties) illegal under WTO rules. Proponents claim this infringes on Congress’s constitutional authority to regulate commerce. The organization’s most-favored-nation principle and thick rulebook are said to limit Washington’s ability to use trade as a strategic tool against adversaries (especially China). Bilateral negotiations, by contrast, allow the US to leverage its massive market size directly rather than dilute that leverage inside a multilateral consensus body.

2. Economic Advantage

The claim here is that these organizations lock the US into arrangements that produce persistent economic losses.

  • UN-related economic arguments are usually secondary but focus on opportunity costs: funds sent to the UN and its specialized agencies (WHO, UNESCO, UNRWA, etc.) could be redirected to domestic priorities or targeted bilateral aid that advances US interests more directly. Critics also argue that UN development and climate mechanisms push regulatory and financial burdens onto wealthy nations while granting developing countries both aid and exemptions, effectively acting as a wealth-transfer system with little accountability for results.

  • WTO draws sharper economic criticism. After China’s 2001 accession, US manufacturing employment declined sharply, trade deficits with China ballooned, and Beijing is accused of exploiting WTO rules through subsidies, forced technology transfer, state-owned enterprises, and intellectual-property theft while enjoying the benefits of open Western markets. The argument is that the WTO’s reciprocal liberalization model assumes all members are playing by roughly similar rules—an assumption falsified by China’s economic system. Withdrawal or dismantling would allow the US to:

    • Impose reciprocal or higher tariffs on countries with unfair practices.
    • Negotiate bilateral or “plurilateral” deals that secure better market access for American exporters and stronger protections for US industries and workers.
    • Use tariffs as a revenue source and bargaining chip without having to justify every measure before international tribunals.

Proponents often cite the post-WWII trade boom under GATT as successful, but argue the modern WTO has become too rigid, slow, and captured by members who do not share free-market premises.

3. Reducing Bureaucratic Constraints and Inefficiency

Both organizations are portrayed as textbook examples of international bureaucracy: slow, expensive, resistant to reform, and prone to mission creep.

  • United Nations: Critics point to duplicated agencies, scandals, waste, and anti-American or ideological bias in staffing and resolutions. Peacekeeping operations have a mixed record and sometimes involve forces from countries with poor human-rights records. Decision-making is cumbersome; even modest reforms have proven nearly impossible because authoritarian or anti-Western states hold veto power over changes. A US exit is presented as a way to escape an unreformable system that still consumes significant American diplomatic bandwidth and money.

  • World Trade Organization: Dispute resolution can take years—sometimes a decade when appeals are stacked. The organization has been unable to conclude major new multilateral agreements for decades (Doha Round collapse). Its rulebook is seen as outdated for digital trade, services, and state capitalism. Critics argue the US is better off operating outside the constraints of consensus-based negotiation and instead using its economic weight to set standards through bilateral pressure, regional deals (USMCA style), or unilateral Section 301/232 tariffs when necessary. This reduces “bureaucratic drag” and allows faster policy response to changing economic realities.

Additional Contextual Claims

  • Historical obsolescence: Both the UN and WTO were shaped by the immediate post-1945 or post-Cold War environments. Today’s distribution of global power (rise of China, India, demographic shifts) is said to make the original designs inequitable or unworkable for the US.
  • Leverage and deterrence: Exiting or threatening to dismantle these bodies is viewed as a way to force reform or replacement with leaner, more interest-based alternatives (e.g., a “League of Democracies,” bilateral trade pacts, or simply ad-hoc coalitions).
  • Domestic political accountability: Supporters argue that Americans should debate and vote on trade-offs directly through their own institutions rather than having them pre-decided in Geneva or New York.

These arguments are most prominently associated with nationalist-conservative thinkers, parts of the Trump administration’s trade and foreign-policy team, and analysts at institutions such as the Heritage Foundation or the America First Policy Institute. They remain highly contested: mainstream international-relations scholars and many business groups counter that the US gains substantial absolute benefits from the stability, predictability, and lower transaction costs provided by these institutions, and that unilateral withdrawal would damage America’s alliances and soft power while inviting rivals to rewrite the rules in even less favorable ways.

Reclaiming Sovereignty: The Case for American Disengagement from the UN and WTO

For the better part of the post-World War II era, the United States operated under a consensus that global engagement was best achieved through multilateral institutions. The debate over the United States' role in multilateral institutions like the United Nations (UN) and the World Trade Organization (WTO) is a longstanding issue in international relations. While supporters of these organizations argue they are essential for global stability and advancing US interests, critics—including advocates for US withdrawal or dismantling—contend that they undermine American self-determination and economic competitiveness.

The arguments for withdrawing from or dismantling these organizations generally revolve around three primary pillars: sovereignty, economic advantage, and the reduction of bureaucratic constraints.

1. Sovereignty and Self-Determination

The argument from sovereignty centers on the belief that international organizations infringe on the United States' ability to govern itself freely. Proponents of withdrawal argue that:

  • Overrides on Domestic Law: Critics point to instances where international rulings conflict with US domestic laws or judicial decisions. For example, WTO dispute panels have ruled against US trade remedies, such as anti-dumping/countervailing duties or the Leveling the Playing Field Act (Section 232 tariffs on steel and aluminum). Critics view these rulings as an affront to US sovereignty, arguing that unelected international judges should not have the authority to force the US to repeal laws enacted by its elected representatives.
  • Normative Pressure and Policy Constraints: In the case of the UN, critics argue that the organization often employs moral equivalence or normative pressure that limits US diplomatic freedom. Resolutions passed by the UN General Assembly or Human Rights Council—which the US has frequently opposed—are seen by some as attempts by hostile or rival nations to constrain US policy in areas such as defense, intelligence, or domestic justice.
  • Control Over Borders and Immigration: Some advocates of withdrawal argue that international bodies, including UN agencies like the UNHCR (Refugee Agency), promote international norms that necessitate open-border or refugee-sharing policies which conflict with the US government's sovereign right to control its own borders and immigration laws.

2. Economic Advantage and Trade Fairness

Arguments regarding economic advantage focus on the belief that multilateral institutions often disadvantage the US economically, favoring developing nations or geopolitical rivals. The primary arguments include:

  • The "Free Rider" Problem and Assessments: The US is the largest financial contributor to the UN, historically paying roughly 22% of the regular budget and a higher percentage of peacekeeping operations. Advocates for withdrawal argue this is economically inequitable, especially since other wealthy economies and emerging global rivals contribute far less. They contend the US could better allocate these billions of dollars toward domestic infrastructure, defense, or debt reduction.
  • Structural Unfairness in Trade (WTO): Regarding the WTO, critics argue that the "special and differential treatment" offered to self-declared developing countries—such as China and India—is outdated and unfair. They assert that the WTO's framework forces the US to maintain open markets while allowing other countries to retain high tariffs, non-tariff barriers, and state subsidies, resulting in chronic trade deficits.
  • Preference for Bilateralism: Proponents of leaving the WTO argue that the US is the world's largest and most dynamic market, giving it immense leverage. Rather than negotiating complex, multilateral deals that require compromise among 164 member states, the US could secure more advantageous terms through bilateral trade agreements where it can fully exploit its market power.

3. Reducing Bureaucratic Constraints

The argument against bureaucracy centers on the inefficiency, sluggishness, and unaccountability of massive multilateral institutions:

  • Gridlock and Sluggishness: International organizations operate on consensus or complex voting procedures. In the UN Security Council, the veto power of rival nations (like Russia and China) frequently paralyzes action, rendering the body ineffective. In the WTO, the consensus-based approach has largely stalled multilateral negotiations (such as the Doha Round), leading critics to view the organization as stagnant and incapable of adapting to modern economic realities like the digital economy.
  • Inefficiency and Bloated Bureaucracy: Critics frequently point to the bureaucratic bloat, high costs, and lack of accountability within international organizations. They argue that the UN, for instance, suffers from overlapping mandates, redundant agencies, and a lack of transparency, leading to wasted funding. Similarly, the WTO’s Appellate Body was criticized by the US for overstepping its mandate, altering the legal standing of members through judicial activism rather than adhering simply to the interpretation of trade agreements.
  • Unilateral Agility: Proponents of withdrawal argue that the US is most effective when it can act swiftly and unilaterally under its own constitutional framework. Instead of wading through layers of international bureaucracy to form a response to a global crisis, the US could form "coalitions of the willing" with like-minded nations, allowing for rapid, decisive action without the procedural constraints of the UN or WTO.

Counter-Perspectives

It is important to note that these arguments face significant counterpoints. Opponents of withdrawal argue that dismantling or leaving these institutions does not eliminate the underlying issues of global economics and security, but rather cedes influence and rule-making power to strategic rivals like China and Russia. They contend that:

  • Sovereignty is Amplified by Engagement: By shaping international rules from within, the US protects its sovereignty better than it would by standing on the outside, where rules are made without its input.
  • Economic Stability: Bilateralism may yield better deals for the short term, but a rules-based multilateral trading system provides the predictability, stability, and supply chain security that have underpinned global economic growth, including US growth.
  • Necessity of Institutions: While bureaucracies can be slow, they serve as vital forums for crisis management, lowering the threshold for international cooperation and preventing conflicts from escalating into larger wars.

Ultimately, the debate over these organizations reflects a fundamental tension in US foreign policy between the desire for absolute independence and the realities of global interdependence.

The Case for American Sovereignty: Why the United States Should Withdraw From the United Nations and the World Trade Organization

Introduction

For more than seven decades the United States has been a cornerstone of the post‑war international order, underwriting institutions such as the United Nations (UN) and the World Trade Organization (WTO) with billions of dollars, military commitments, and diplomatic capital. The promise was simple: by pooling sovereignty in multilateral bodies, the world would become safer, more prosperous, and more just. Today, however, the evidence tells a different story. These organizations have become arenas where American interests are routinely subordinated to the agendas of rival powers, where bureaucratic fiat overrides democratic accountability, and where the very concept of national sovereignty is eroded. The time has come for the United States to reclaim its sovereign prerogatives by actively dismantling its membership in the UN and the WTO—or, at a minimum, withdrawing from them—so that it can pursue policies that truly serve its citizens, its economy, and its security.

I. The Erosion of American Sovereignty

A. Legal and Political Constraints Imposed by International Bodies

  1. Binding Resolutions and Treaties – The UN Security Council can authorize the use of force, impose sanctions, and create binding legal obligations that the United States must follow, even when those actions conflict with domestic law or the will of the American people. The 2003 Iraq War, for instance, was launched without a UN mandate, yet the subsequent occupation was constrained by UN resolutions that limited U.S. operational flexibility.

  2. WTO Dispute‑Resolution Mechanisms – The WTO’s Appellate Body can overturn U.S. trade laws, forcing Congress to weaken environmental, labor, or safety standards to avoid costly retaliation. The 2019 ruling against the U.S. “Country‑of‑Origin Labeling” (COOL) regime illustrates how a supranational tribunal can dictate domestic policy.

  3. Loss of Legislative Autonomy – By ceding decision‑making authority to international secretariats, the U.S. Congress is effectively bypassed. The President can invoke “international obligations” to justify executive actions—such as the Paris Climate Agreement—without the explicit consent of the legislature, undermining the constitutional separation of powers.

B. The “One‑Size‑Fits‑All” Approach Ignores American Particularities

International organizations operate on consensus‑based or majority‑rule models that reflect the interests of the global majority, not the unique economic, cultural, and security needs of the United States. Policies crafted in Geneva or New York often prioritize developing‑world concerns—such as agricultural subsidies for smallholder farmers—at the expense of America’s high‑tech, service‑oriented economy.

II. Economic Costs and Missed Opportunities

A. Trade Deficits and Unfair Competition

  1. WTO’s “Most‑Favored‑Nation” Principle – While the principle is theoretically non‑discriminatory, it has allowed countries like China and India to maintain protectionist practices (e.g., state‑backed subsidies, forced technology transfer) while the United States abides by open‑market rules. The result: a persistent U.S. trade deficit that has cost millions of manufacturing jobs.

  2. Regulatory Arbitrage – Multinational corporations exploit WTO rules to shift production to low‑wage jurisdictions, undercutting American workers. The “Investor‑State Dispute Settlement” (ISDS) mechanisms further empower foreign firms to challenge U.S. regulations, chilling domestic policymaking.

B. Fiscal Drain of Membership Fees

  • UN Budget: The United States contributes roughly 22 % of the UN’s regular budget—approximately $1.5 billion annually—plus additional assessments for peacekeeping missions. These funds could be redirected toward domestic infrastructure, education, or defense modernization.
  • WTO Budget: Although smaller, U.S. contributions to the WTO’s Technical Cooperation and Dispute Settlement funds still amount to hundreds of millions of dollars that could be better spent on trade‑promotion initiatives tailored to American exporters.

C. Missed Bilateral Opportunities

By anchoring its trade policy in multilateral frameworks, Washington forfeits the agility to negotiate swift, tailored deals with key partners. Bilateral agreements—such as the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement (USMCA)—demonstrate that the U.S. can secure favorable terms without ceding authority to a global body that often stalls progress.

III. Security and Strategic Implications

A. UN Security Council Vetoes as a Diplomatic Straitjacket

The veto power of the five permanent members frequently paralyzes collective action, leaving the United States to act unilaterally—or not at all—when crises arise. The inability to secure a UN mandate for interventions in Syria, Libya, and the South China Sea has forced Washington to either bypass the organization (risking international legitimacy) or accept inaction (undermining its strategic interests).

B. Peacekeeping Missions and Mission Creep

U.S. troops have been deployed under UN command in missions that lack clear exit strategies or alignment with American security objectives. The prolonged involvement in the Democratic Republic of Congo, for example, has entangled U.S. forces in a complex web of regional rivalries without a direct benefit to homeland security.

C. Intelligence and Technology Sharing Risks

Participation in multilateral intelligence frameworks (e.g., the UN’s Counter‑Terrorism Committee) necessitates sharing sensitive data with states that may not share America’s values or security priorities. Such exchanges can be exploited by adversaries, as evidenced by the inadvertent transfer of dual‑use technology through UN‑sanctioned research programs.

IV. The Myth of “International Leadership”

Proponents of multilateralism argue that U.S. participation projects soft power and ensures a rules‑based order. Yet recent history shows that leadership is more effectively exercised through coalitions of the willing and bilateral partnerships than through cumbersome, consensus‑driven bureaucracies.

  • NATO remains a robust, treaty‑based alliance that operates without UN oversight, demonstrating that security cooperation can thrive outside the UN framework.
  • The Quad (U.S., Japan, India, Australia) and the AUKUS pact illustrate how like‑minded democracies can address Indo‑Pacific security challenges more nimbly than the UN’s plenary sessions.

When the United States leads from a position of sovereign strength, it can set the agenda rather than be forced to compromise on core interests.

V. Countering the “Isolationist” Label

Critics will brand a withdrawal as isolationism, but the argument here is not for retreat from the world; it is for strategic engagement on terms that protect American sovereignty. The United States can:

  1. Forge Ad Hoc Coalitions – Build issue‑specific alliances (e.g., climate‑technology partnerships, cybersecurity pacts) that do not require ceding decision‑making to a global body.
  2. Lead Through Bilateral Agreements – Negotiate trade deals that reflect American standards, rather than accepting lowest‑common‑denominator WTO rules.
  3. Maintain Selective Participation – Remain observer or associate member in bodies where U.S. interests align, while retaining the right to opt out of binding decisions.

VI. A Roadmap for Withdrawal

Step Action Rationale
1️⃣ Announce Intent – Issue a presidential executive order outlining the intent to withdraw from the UN and WTO, citing sovereignty and fiscal concerns. Provides legal notice and initiates the required procedural timelines (e.g., one‑year notice for WTO).
2️⃣ Renegotiate Bilateral Agreements – Initiate talks with key allies (EU, Japan, Australia, Canada) to replace multilateral frameworks with reciprocal trade and security pacts. Ensures continuity of economic and security relationships without multilateral constraints.
3️⃣ Redirect Funds – Allocate the saved UN/WTO contributions to domestic infrastructure, defense modernization, and innovation hubs. Demonstrates tangible benefits to American taxpayers.
4️⃣ Establish a “Sovereignty Council” – Create an inter‑agency body to evaluate future international engagements, ensuring each commitment passes a strict cost‑benefit and sovereignty impact test. Institutionalizes the principle that American interests come first.
5️⃣ Public Diplomacy Campaign – Communicate the rationale to the American public and the international community, emphasizing that the U.S. remains a reliable partner but will not cede its constitutional authority. Builds domestic support and mitigates diplomatic fallout.

Conclusion

The United Nations and the World Trade Organization were conceived in an era when multilateral cooperation seemed the surest path to peace and prosperity. In the 21st century, however, these institutions have morphed into constraints on American sovereignty, drains on the federal budget, and obstacles to the agile, bilateral strategies that best protect U.S. interests. By withdrawing—or at minimum dismantling the binding obligations that these bodies impose—the United States can reassert its sovereign authority, redirect resources to priorities that directly benefit its citizens, and lead the world through dynamic, like‑minded partnerships rather than through cumbersome, one‑size‑fits‑all bureaucracies. The choice is not between isolation and engagement; it is between engagement on America’s terms and submission to a global order that no longer serves the American people. Reclaiming American Sovereignty: The Case for Withdrawing from International Organizations

Introduction

For decades, American foreign policy has operated under the assumption that membership in sprawling international organizations serves the national interest. The United Nations, World Trade Organization, and similar multilateral bodies have been treated as sacrosanct pillars of the "rules-based international order." Yet a clear-eyed assessment reveals a troubling reality: these institutions increasingly function as constraints on American self-governance, wealth transfers to hostile or ungrateful nations, and mechanisms through which foreign powers seek to contain and diminish American strength. The time has come for the United States to fundamentally reassess—and ultimately withdraw from—these organizations that no longer serve the American people.

The Sovereignty Imperative

Constitutional Foundations

The United States Constitution established a revolutionary principle: that governmental legitimacy derives from the consent of the governed, expressed through elected representatives accountable to citizens. Article I vests legislative power in Congress. Article II places executive authority in an elected President. Nowhere does the Constitution contemplate the surrender of these powers to international bureaucracies staffed by unelected foreign officials.

Yet this surrender has occurred through incremental erosion. When the WTO Appellate Body rules against American trade laws, it effectively exercises judicial review over congressional legislation—a power the Constitution reserves exclusively to American courts interpreting American law. When UN treaty bodies issue "interpretations" of conventions the United States has signed, they attempt to bind American policy without any vote by American legislators. When UN Security Council resolutions purport to obligate American action, they circumvent the constitutional requirement that treaties receive Senate ratification by a two-thirds supermajority.

This is not abstract legal theorizing. These encroachments have concrete consequences. American workers, businesses, and communities find their lives governed by decisions made in Geneva and New York by officials they never elected, cannot remove from office, and who bear no accountability to them whatsoever.

The Democratic Deficit

International organizations suffer from a fundamental democratic deficit that cannot be reformed away—it is inherent in their structure. Consider the UN General Assembly, where each nation receives one vote regardless of population, wealth, or commitment to human rights. The United States, with 330 million citizens and the world's largest economy, holds the same voting power as nations with populations smaller than American cities. This arrangement would be considered absurdly undemocratic if applied domestically, yet Americans are expected to accept it as the foundation of "international law."

The WTO compounds this problem with a dispute settlement system that operates in secret, applies vague treaty language according to the preferences of unaccountable judges, and produces rulings that override domestic democratic choices. When American voters elect representatives who enact trade policies to protect domestic industries or promote national security, WTO tribunals can invalidate those choices with no avenue for democratic appeal.

True self-governance requires that the people affected by decisions have meaningful control over those decisions. International organizations systematically sever this connection, transferring power from accountable domestic institutions to unaccountable international ones.

The Failure to Serve American Interests

The United Nations: A Record of Dysfunction

The United Nations was founded with a noble purpose: preventing another world war and promoting international peace. Judged by this standard, its record is deeply unimpressive. The UN failed to prevent wars in Korea, Vietnam, the Balkans, Rwanda, Iraq, Syria, Yemen, Ukraine, and countless other conflicts. The Security Council's veto structure ensures paralysis on any matter involving great power interests, rendering the body useless precisely when it matters most.

Meanwhile, the UN has metastasized into a vast bureaucracy that serves the institutional interests of its employees and the political agendas of member states hostile to America and its allies. Consider the UN Human Rights Council, which has included among its members China, Cuba, Venezuela, Russia, and Saudi Arabia—nations with atrocious human rights records that cynically use their positions to deflect criticism and attack democracies. Israel, America's closest ally in the Middle East and the region's only genuine democracy, has been the subject of more Human Rights Council resolutions than all other countries combined. This is not oversight; it is systematic bias.

The UN Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA), ostensibly a humanitarian organization for Palestinian refugees, has been repeatedly exposed harboring Hamas militants, storing weapons in its facilities, and promoting antisemitic content in its educational materials. American taxpayers have been the largest funders of this organization for decades.

UNESCO has been used as a platform for anti-American and anti-Israel propaganda, including declarations implicitly denying Jewish historical connections to Jerusalem. The UN Conference on Trade and Development pushes economic policies directly contrary to free-market principles that have generated American prosperity.

For all of this, the United States pays approximately 22% of the UN regular budget and 27% of peacekeeping costs—by far the largest share of any nation. American taxpayers subsidize an organization that routinely acts against American interests and values.

The WTO: Enabling America's Decline

The World Trade Organization was sold to the American public as a mechanism for opening foreign markets to American exports while establishing fair rules for international commerce. The reality has been starkly different.

The WTO's most consequential decision was facilitating China's accession in 2001. Proponents promised that integrating China into the global trading system would liberalize its economy and eventually its political system. Instead, China exploited WTO membership to access Western markets while maintaining massive state subsidies, forced technology transfers, intellectual property theft, currency manipulation, and other mercantilist practices that the WTO's cumbersome procedures proved utterly incapable of addressing.

The results speak for themselves. Between 2001 and 2015, the United States lost an estimated 3.4 million jobs to Chinese import competition, according to economists David Autor, David Dorn, and Gordon Hanson. Entire communities in the American heartland were devastated as manufacturing fled to China. The WTO not only failed to prevent this catastrophe—it enabled and legitimized it.

When the United States has attempted to defend itself through trade remedies, WTO dispute panels have frequently ruled against American measures. The Appellate Body consistently interpreted WTO agreements to maximize constraints on American policy flexibility. Between 1995 and 2020, the United States lost approximately 90% of cases brought against it at the WTO—a record that suggests systemic bias rather than American lawlessness.

The WTO fundamentally misconceives the purpose of trade policy. Trade should serve the national interest—promoting prosperity, maintaining strategic industries, and preserving national security. The WTO treats trade liberalization as an end in itself, regardless of whether trading partners reciprocate or whether the consequences serve American workers and communities. This ideological rigidity has proven disastrous.

Structural Problems Beyond Reform

Institutional Capture and Bureaucratic Interests

International organizations develop institutional interests distinct from—and often opposed to—the interests of their member states. UN bureaucracies seek to expand their budgets, authority, and permanence regardless of whether their activities produce results. This creates pressure for mission creep, with organizations continually discovering new problems requiring their intervention and expanded resources.

The phenomenon of institutional capture compounds this problem. Countries hostile to American interests and values have systematically placed their nationals in key positions throughout the UN system. These officials then use their positions to advance their countries' agendas under the legitimizing cover of "international" authority.

Specialized agencies have been captured by ideological movements that oppose American values. UN Women promotes radical gender ideology. The UN Environment Programme has become a platform for climate alarmism and anti-capitalist economics. The World Health Organization's handling of COVID-19—including its deference to Chinese government narratives during the critical early weeks of the pandemic—demonstrated how institutional capture can produce catastrophic consequences.

The Impossibility of Reform

Defenders of international organizations acknowledge these problems but invariably argue that the solution is reform rather than withdrawal. This argument misconceives the nature of the problem. The dysfunction of international organizations is not incidental—it is inherent in their structure.

Reform requires consensus among member states, many of whom benefit from current arrangements and have no interest in changes that would serve American interests. The UN can never be reformed to be meaningfully accountable to democratic principles because most of its members are not democracies and have no interest in democratic accountability. The WTO cannot be reformed to allow robust defense of American interests because its entire purpose, as conceived by its architects and member states, is to constrain such measures.

Decades of American efforts at reform have produced negligible results. The Reagan administration withheld UN dues to demand reforms; the organization waited out American pressure and resumed business as usual once funding resumed. The Trump administration withdrew from various UN bodies and blocked WTO Appellate Body appointments; the Biden administration reversed these policies without extracting meaningful reforms. The pattern is clear: international organizations are structured to resist American pressure for change.

The Alternative: Strategic Flexibility and Bilateral Arrangements

Reclaiming Policy Space

Withdrawal from international organizations would reclaim the policy flexibility the United States needs to navigate an increasingly competitive and dangerous world. Trade policy could be designed to serve American workers rather than abstract principles of liberalization. Immigration policy could be set according to national interest without UN committees issuing pronouncements about American obligations. Environmental policy could balance economic and environmental concerns without the dictates of international bureaucracies.

This is not isolationism. The United States would remain deeply engaged with the world—but on terms that serve American interests. Engagement would be selective, strategic, and accountable to the American people through their elected representatives.

Bilateral and Minilateral Alternatives

International organizations are not the only—or even the best—mechanism for international cooperation. Bilateral agreements between the United States and individual partners can be tailored to specific circumstances and negotiated to produce genuinely reciprocal benefits. When the United States negotiates directly with a trading partner, it brings the full weight of the world's largest economy to bear; in multilateral settings, this leverage is diluted.

Where multilateral cooperation serves American interests, it can be organized through coalitions of nations that share American values and interests—what might be called minilateralism. NATO, despite its imperfections, demonstrates that security cooperation among democracies can be effective. The Quad (United States, Japan, India, Australia) represents a promising model for strategic cooperation in the Indo-Pacific. These arrangements allow cooperation without surrendering sovereignty to universal organizations dominated by non-democracies and hostile powers.

Precedent and Feasibility

American withdrawal from international organizations is neither unprecedented nor impractical. The United States has withdrawn from UNESCO twice (1984-2003 and 2018-2023). It withdrew from the UN Human Rights Council under the Trump administration. It effectively paralyzed the WTO Appellate Body by refusing to approve new judges. In none of these cases did the predicted catastrophes materialize. The world continued to function. American interests were arguably better served than during periods of membership.

More dramatically, the United Kingdom's withdrawal from the European Union demonstrates that even deep integration can be reversed when the democratic will demands it. Brexit was fiercely opposed by establishment opinion, yet Britain extracted itself from EU institutions and has not collapsed into chaos. This example should give pause to those who argue that American withdrawal from international organizations is inconceivable.

Addressing Counterarguments

"The US Shaped These Institutions"

It is true that the United States played the leading role in creating the post-World War II international order. But institutions designed for the world of 1945—with the United States representing half of global GDP, Western Europe in ruins, and the Soviet Union as the primary adversary—are not necessarily suited to the world of 2025, with a rising China, resurgent Russia, and American economic dominance diminished.

More importantly, the institutions themselves have changed. The UN of 1945, with 51 member states dominated by Western democracies, is fundamentally different from the UN of today, with 193 members and an automatic anti-American majority in the General Assembly. The GATT trading system that served American interests reasonably well has been transformed into a WTO that constrains American policy while failing to discipline Chinese mercantilism. Nostalgia for the institutions America created should not blind us to what those institutions have become.

"Withdrawal Would Damage American Influence"

This argument assumes that membership in international organizations translates into influence. The evidence suggests otherwise. Despite being the largest funder of the UN, the United States is routinely outvoted and its positions ignored. Despite being the largest market in the world, the United States loses case after case at the WTO.

True influence derives from power—economic, military, and diplomatic. The United States possesses these in abundance and would retain them regardless of organizational memberships. Indeed, withdrawal might enhance American influence by forcing other nations to deal with the United States directly rather than using international organizations to constrain and outvote it.

"We Need These Organizations to Address Global Problems"

Some problems genuinely require international coordination. But international organizations have proven remarkably ineffective at addressing them. The UN failed to prevent climate change, stop pandemics, end poverty, or prevent war. The WTO failed to liberalize China or create a fair trading system. These organizations excel at holding conferences, issuing reports, and expanding their own bureaucracies. They have been far less successful at solving actual problems.

Where international cooperation is genuinely necessary—and it sometimes is—it can be organized ad hoc among willing participants rather than through permanent bureaucracies with their own agendas. The most effective international responses to emergencies have typically come from coalitions of capable and willing states, not from UN resolutions.

Conclusion: A New Declaration of Independence

The American Revolution was, at its core, a declaration that the American people would govern themselves rather than submit to distant authorities that did not represent them. The fundamental principle—that legitimate government derives from the consent of the governed—remains as valid today as in 1776.

International organizations represent a return to the pre-revolutionary condition. They place authority over American lives in the hands of bureaucracies the American people did not elect, cannot remove, and over which they exercise no meaningful control. They transfer American wealth to nations that seek to constrain American power. They subject American policy to rules designed by foreign governments to serve foreign interests.

The path forward requires a new declaration of independence—not from any foreign king, but from the web of international institutions that have gradually enmeshed American sovereignty. The United States should systematically evaluate each international organization and treaty commitment, withdrawing from those that fail to serve American interests and reforming or replacing those that can be salvaged.

This is not a retreat from the world. It is an assertion that American engagement with the world will be conducted on American terms, accountable to the American people, and in service of American interests. It is a recognition that sovereignty—the right of a people to govern themselves—is not an outdated concept to be traded away for the approval of globalist elites, but the foundation of legitimate government and the birthright of every American citizen.

The choice before us is clear: continued submission to institutions that undermine our self-governance and fail to serve our interests, or the reclamation of the sovereignty our founders fought to establish. For those who believe that the American people should control their own destiny, there can be only one answer.

Two hundred and forty-eight years ago, our founders pledged their lives, their fortunes, and their sacred honor to establish something revolutionary: a nation governed not by distant monarchs, but by the consent of the governed. They believed—and fought and died for the belief—that Americans should determine their own destiny.

Today, I stand before you to ask a simple question: Who governs America?

Is it you? Is it the representatives you elect? Or is it unelected bureaucrats in Geneva, in Brussels, in glass towers along the East River—people who have never walked your streets, never met your families, never understood your struggles?

The answer should trouble every American who loves liberty.

The Sovereignty We've Surrendered

Let me be clear about what we've given away.

The United Nations—founded with noble aspirations—has become a forum where dictatorships lecture democracies on human rights. Where the Human Rights Council has included nations that stone women, imprison journalists, and crush dissent. Where our tax dollars—billions of them—fund agencies riddled with inefficiency, corruption, and anti-American bias.

We send more money to the UN than any other nation. And what do we receive? Resolutions condemning our ally Israel more times than every other nation combined. Lectures from autocrats. And a Security Council paralyzed by the vetoes of nations that oppose everything we stand for.

The World Trade Organization promised free and fair trade. Instead, it created a system where China—a nation that manipulates its currency, steals intellectual property, and subsidizes state industries—has been allowed to hollow out American manufacturing. While WTO tribunals second-guess our laws, American workers watched their factories close, their towns decay, their futures evaporate.

We were told globalization would lift all boats. But someone forgot to tell the families in Ohio, in Michigan, in Pennsylvania, whose boats sank while the architects of this system grew wealthy.

The Myth of "International Community"

We're told we must remain in these institutions because of the "international community." But let me ask you: What community?

A community shares values. It shares burdens. It comes to each other's defense.

When American soldiers are asked to keep the peace, where is this community? When American taxpayers fund global health initiatives, disaster relief, peacekeeping operations—where is the gratitude, let alone the reciprocity?

The "international community" is too often a phrase used to constrain American action while excusing the failures of others. It's invoked to guilt us into agreements that bind us while others cheat. It's wielded as a weapon against our sovereignty by those who could never build what our founders built.

We don't need the approval of the international community. We need to rediscover our own national purpose.

The Democratic Deficit

Here is the heart of my argument, and I want every American to understand it:

These institutions are fundamentally undemocratic.

When the WTO overrules American law, who voted for that? When UN treaties are cited to influence our courts, who consented? When international bodies claim authority over our environmental policy, our trade policy, our immigration policy—where is the accountability?

You cannot vote out a WTO judge. You cannot recall a UN commissioner. You cannot hold a referendum on decisions made in closed rooms by people who answer to no electorate.

Our Constitution begins with three sacred words: "We the People." Not "We the International Bodies." Not "We the Global Consensus." We the People.

Every commitment that transfers authority away from our elected government is a theft from you—a theft of the self-governance your ancestors fought to establish and preserve.

The Case for Withdrawal

Some say withdrawal would isolate us. I say it would liberate us.

Without the WTO's constraints, we could finally demand true reciprocity in trade. If China wants access to American consumers, they will meet American standards—or they will not have access. Simple. Fair. American.

Without UN entanglements, we could redirect those billions to our veterans, to our infrastructure, to our borders. We could engage in diplomacy on our terms, forming alliances based on shared interests rather than institutional obligation.

Withdrawal is not isolation. It is independence.

We would still trade. We would still negotiate. We would still engage. But we would do so as a sovereign nation, not as a supplicant to institutions that have failed their missions.

What They'll Say

The establishment will call this dangerous. They'll say we'll lose influence. They'll invoke chaos and catastrophe.

But consider: these same voices told us NAFTA would be an unqualified success. They told us admitting China to the WTO would liberalize their system. They told us nation-building in distant lands would be quick and easy. They told us the experts knew best.

They were wrong. Again and again, they were wrong. And yet they expect us to keep trusting their judgment over our own.

The institutions they defend have not prevented wars. They have not stopped nuclear proliferation. They have not lifted billions from poverty—free enterprise did that. They have not protected human rights in the places where they're most abused.

What they have done is create comfortable careers for diplomats, lucrative positions for bureaucrats, and endless conferences in pleasant cities—all funded substantially by you, the American taxpayer.

A Return to First Principles

I'm not calling for America to retreat from the world. I'm calling for America to engage with the world as America—confident, sovereign, and free.

Bilateral agreements with nations that share our values. Hard bargaining with those that don't. Aid given freely where it advances our interests, not mandated by institutions that squander it. Alliances based on mutual commitment, not bureaucratic inertia.

This is not radical. This is what international relations looked like for most of human history. And it is what our founders intended.

Jefferson warned against "entangling alliances." Washington counseled independence from foreign influence. They understood what we have forgotten: that sovereignty, once surrendered, is rarely recovered without sacrifice.

The Choice Before Us

My fellow Americans, we stand at a crossroads.

One path leads deeper into a web of international obligations, further diluting your voice, further empowering unaccountable institutions, further binding our nation to the failures and compromises of a "global order" that serves everyone but you.

The other path leads home. To a government accountable to its citizens. To an economy that serves its workers. To a nation that determines its own destiny.

The establishment will fight this. The comfortable will resist. Those who profit from the current system will call us every name they can imagine.

Let them.

Because this movement isn't about ideology. It's about something deeper. It's about whether America will remain America—a self-governing republic where the people rule.

I believe in that America. I believe you do too.

It's time to bring our sovereignty home. It's time to withdraw from institutions that constrain without benefiting us. It's time to remind the world—and ourselves—that America bows to no foreign body, answers to no external authority, and charts its own course among the nations.

Our founders declared independence once. Now it falls to us to reclaim it.

Thank you, God bless you, and God bless the United States of America.
